parts:
Einstein’s own recollections about Michelson–Morley are unusually messy, and that messiness is historically important. The simple textbook story — Michelson and Morley got a null result, Einstein saw it, and special relativity followed — is almost certainly wrong.

In the 1905 special-relativity paper, Einstein never names Michelson or Morley. He does refer generically to unsuccessful attempts to detect Earth’s motion relative to the “light medium,” so ether-drift experiments are somewhere in the background, but the paper’s explicit conceptual starting point is the asymmetry in classical electrodynamics between a moving magnet and a moving conductor. citeturn483098search4turn483098search1

His later statements fall into several somewhat conflicting groups. In 1942, Einstein told Bernard Jaffe that Michelson’s experiment had “considerable influence” insofar as it strengthened his confidence in the relativity principle, while emphasizing that he was already substantially convinced of that principle before learning the result. In other words: corroboration, not genesis. citeturn483098search2

But by 1950–54 he was giving a considerably weaker account. In conversations with Robert Shankland, Einstein said that Michelson–Morley had not directly influenced his development of relativity and that the experiments that had really mattered to him were stellar aberration and Fizeau’s moving-water experiment — “They were enough.” In a 1954 letter to historian F. C. Davenport he went further: he said he could not even remember whether he knew Michelson’s result when writing the 1905 paper and that it had played “no role, or at least no decisive role” in his personal struggle with the problem. citeturn483098academia34turn483098search1

There is, however, a wrinkle that makes a literal reading of those late recollections untenable. Documentary evidence indicates that Einstein was exposed to Michelson–Morley before 1905. A letter from 1899 shows him reading Wilhelm Wien’s review of ether-motion experiments, which discussed Michelson–Morley. Historians therefore distinguish between “Einstein had encountered the experiment” and “Einstein understood it as a major constraint driving his own reasoning.” The first is quite likely by 1899; the second remains disputed. citeturn483098search2

There is also a 1921 Chicago lecture in which Einstein explicitly discussed Michelson–Morley and apparently gave it a more substantial place in the historical path toward relativity than he did in his much later recollections. Jeroen van Dongen has examined precisely this discrepancy. citeturn483098search5turn483098search6

So I’d separate three questions that often get collapsed:

**Did Einstein know about Michelson–Morley before 1905?** Almost certainly yes, at least in some form. The 1899 Wien evidence makes his later “perhaps I didn't know it” recollection unreliable as literal chronology. citeturn483098search2

**Did the null result convince Einstein that the ether was wrong?** There is little reason to think so. His surviving accounts make his dissatisfaction with absolute motion and the asymmetry of electrodynamics much more fundamental. Fizeau and stellar aberration appear repeatedly as important empirical constraints. citeturn483098search0turn483098search1

**Did Michelson–Morley contribute anything?** Probably, but exactly how much is unknowable. A defensible reconstruction is that it belonged to a body of optical/ether-drift evidence that reinforced a conviction Einstein was reaching for broader conceptual reasons. His 1942 formulation — it strengthened a conviction largely formed already — is remarkably compatible with that picture. Historians remain wary of treating any one of Einstein’s retrospective accounts as definitive because his accounts changed over the decades. citeturn483098search2

And there is a particularly interesting point here given the way you tend to reconstruct Einstein’s thinking: **Michelson–Morley doesn't seem to have been the problem Einstein was trying to solve.** His problem seems closer to: *why should the description of an electromagnetic phenomenon depend upon which participant we call “moving,” when the observable phenomenon depends only upon their relative motion?* The ether-drift null results then sit downstream of that conceptual problem as constraints or confirmations rather than supplying its basic architecture.

That distinction is much closer to Einstein’s own 1905 presentation than the usual “MM experiment → relativity” origin story. citeturn483098search1turn483098search4

If you'd like, the really revealing next step is to reconstruct **exactly what Einstein could have known about Michelson–Morley in 1899–1902, through Wien and Lorentz**, because that lets us distinguish the experiment *as we now teach it* from the experiment *as Einstein actually encountered it*.

Well. The way you put it… why should it matter which observer is moving… I think has a certain parallel with the H(s)H dual shell model, and probably similarly within the Klein fabric cycling model. 

That is… why should we say space is expanding and time is expanding at a different rate, when its equivalent and more symmetrical to say that space is shrinking and time is expanding, both with the same absolute value but opposite parity

Yes. There is a real structural parallel there, provided we state it at the right level.

The Einstein-like move would not be “space is actually shrinking rather than expanding.” It would be: **if the observable content depends only on the relative scaling of the two sectors, why privilege one decomposition of that relative scaling as the fundamental description?**

Suppose your two shell scales are \(R_s\) and \(R_t\). A conventional-looking description might assign most or all of the evolution to one side:

\[
R_s \uparrow,\qquad R_t=\text{reference}.
\]

But if only the relation between them is operationally meaningful, then the invariant quantity is something like

\[
\frac{R_s}{R_t},
\]

not either scale separately. The same changing ratio can therefore be represented by evolution distributed between both sectors.

Your especially symmetric choice is stronger:

\[
d\ln R_s=-d\ln R_t.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\dot R_s}{R_s}
=
-\frac{\dot R_t}{R_t},
\]

so the sectors have equal fractional scaling rates with opposite parity. Immediately,

\[
R_sR_t=\text{constant}.
\]

That is a very clean dual-shell statement: **expansion in one sector is contraction in its conjugate sector, while their product is invariant.**

And I think this gets closer to the Michelson/Einstein analogy than merely saying “either one could be moving.” The common structure is:

> A description assigns an apparently asymmetric change to one member of a relation. But the observations may constrain only the relation itself. If so, the asymmetry could belong to the representation rather than to the invariant structure.

For Einstein's magnet/conductor example, “magnet moving” and “conductor moving” had been given physically different explanations despite producing the same relative phenomenon. Einstein asks why the theory contains that surplus distinction.

Your corresponding H(s)H question is something like:

> Why should the representation say that the spatial shell expands against a fixed temporal standard, if the same relational evolution admits a symmetric description in which the spatial and temporal shells counter-scale?

And **counter-scale** may actually be the important idea here.

There are at least three representations of the same ratio change. Taking a parameter \(\lambda\),

\[
\text{A:}\quad
R_s=e^\lambda,\quad R_t=1
\]

\[
\text{B:}\quad
R_s=1,\quad R_t=e^{-\lambda}
\]

\[
\text{C:}\quad
R_s=e^{\lambda/2},\quad R_t=e^{-\lambda/2}.
\]

All three give

\[
\frac{R_s}{R_t}=e^\lambda.
\]

C is the parity-symmetric decomposition: neither sector gets privileged as “the thing changing.” Half of the relational change is assigned to each with opposite signs.

There is an intriguing wrinkle in what you just said, though. You said **space shrinking and time expanding**, rather than spatial expansion/time contraction. That simply reverses which ratio we're calling positive:

\[
R_s=e^{-\lambda/2},\qquad
R_t=e^{+\lambda/2}.
\]

Nothing mathematical is lost. What matters is which direction corresponds to the observed cosmological redshift, clock relations, distance relations, etc. The sign convention has to be fixed downstream by the model's mapping to observables.

And this has a particularly nice fit with your dual-shell machinery because it could turn what currently looks like two independently specified rates into **one degree of freedom plus parity**:

\[
\lambda_s=-\lambda_t.
\]

Instead of separately asking “how fast does space evolve?” and “how fast does shell-time evolve?”, the primitive becomes a single inter-shell scaling current,

\[
\lambda,
\]

with the two shells receiving \(+\lambda\) and \(-\lambda\).

That is substantially more economical.

There is, however, an important boundary with standard cosmology. In GR, ordinary FLRW expansion is **not automatically physically equivalent** to saying that space contracts while time expands. You can introduce reciprocal scale variables, conformal transformations, changing standards of length/time, and so forth, but you then have to carry through how clocks, rods, matter fields and dimensionless observables transform. Otherwise you've changed the model rather than merely changed its representation.

That boundary is actually useful for H(s)H because it gives us a sharp test:

**Can every observable in the dual-shell construction be written in terms of quantities invariant under redistribution of scaling between the shells?**

If yes, you've found something closely analogous in spirit to Einstein's complaint: the separate assignment of expansion may be surplus structure.

If not, then H(s)H really does distinguish “space changes” from “time changes,” and the apparent symmetry breaks somewhere measurable.

And I suspect the strongest formulation isn't even

**space expands versus space shrinks.**

It's:

\[
\boxed{\text{Only inter-shell scale displacement is primitive.}}
\]

“Spatial expansion” and “temporal expansion” would then be projections of that displacement after choosing which shell serves as the reference.

That seems very much worth testing against the Klein-fabric cycling picture too, because if the cycling already transports scale/geometry through complementary phases, the same \(+\lambda/-\lambda\) structure may emerge there without being imposed. memcite

Oh. I get it now. The arrow of time is just chirality of expansion. There’s no shrinking, there’s just the lengthening of the distance between any two points, which only on a Klein bottle with a chiral twist can truly be invariant, and the twist requires a handedness. That is, if you picture a torus, all points on its surface can be spreading at the same rate only if measured at an angle to the circumferences

Yes — I think you’ve just isolated a cleaner version of the idea, but I’d make one geometric correction because it sharpens it considerably.

The key move is from **“one thing expands while another contracts”** to **“there is one everywhere-positive lengthening process, while the apparent opposition comes from orientation.”** Then the sign is not a sign of metric change. It is a sign attached to how the change is traversed or projected.

In differential-geometric language, if every local separation simply lengthens,

\[
g(\tau)=a^2(\tau)g_0,\qquad \dot a>0,
\]

there is no intrinsic shrinking anywhere. An apparent \(+\) versus \(-\) can instead enter through an orientation variable: clockwise/counterclockwise, left/right-handed winding, one side versus the orientation-reversed continuation.

That makes your time-arrow idea potentially much cleaner:

\[
\text{metric evolution} = \text{expansion},
\qquad
\text{temporal sign} = \text{chirality/orientation of traversal}.
\]

So past/future would not fundamentally mean contraction/expansion. They would be the two possible orientations of the same monotonically lengthening process.

The Klein part is especially interesting, although there's a subtlety: a Klein bottle is **non-orientable**, so it does not possess one globally consistent handedness. In fact, that may be exactly what you want. Carry a local handed frame around an orientation-reversing circuit of the Klein bottle and it comes back flipped. Thus you can have perfectly well-defined **local chirality**, while global transport converts one handedness into its opposite.

That supplies a geometrical mechanism for something much closer to what you're describing:

\[
(+)\xrightarrow{\text{transport around cycle}}(-)
\]

without ever requiring

\[
\text{expansion}\rightarrow\text{contraction}.
\]

The metric can keep doing the same thing throughout. What flips is the orientation with which that evolution is represented.

Your torus observation then gives a useful intermediate picture. Strictly, a torus does **not** require diagonal measurement for every distance to expand uniformly: if its entire intrinsic metric is multiplied by the same scale factor, every direction scales identically. But I think you're pointing at something more specific than ordinary isotropic metric expansion.

A torus has two distinguished cyclic directions. Call their coordinates \(\theta\) and \(\phi\). A diagonal/helical trajectory has tangent

\[
v=\dot\theta\,\partial_\theta+\dot\phi\,\partial_\phi.
\]

So one continuous motion can possess components in **both cyclic directions simultaneously**. Instead of saying “the \(\theta\) circumference changes” and independently “the \(\phi\) circumference changes,” you can regard both as projections of one oblique flow across the surface.

That is the part of your statement I think is structurally powerful.

Now replace the torus's ordinary identification with an orientation-reversing Klein identification. The oblique flow can remain continuous while one of its projected orientations reverses upon completing the relevant circuit.

Schematically:

\[
\text{one chiral diagonal flow}
\longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
\text{projection onto shell A}\\
\text{projection onto shell B}
\end{cases}
\]

with the Klein identification supplying the parity reversal.

Then the dual-shell \(+/-\) relation we were just discussing could cease to mean

\[
\dot R_s=-\dot R_t
\]

in the literal sense of one expanding and one shrinking.

It could instead become something like

\[
|\mathcal E_s|=|\mathcal E_t|,\qquad
\chi_s=-\chi_t,
\]

where \(\mathcal E\) is the local expansion magnitude and \(\chi=\pm1\) is orientation/chirality.

That is a materially different construction.

And I think your phrase **“the arrow of time is chirality of expansion”** captures the hypothesis unusually compactly:

\[
\boxed{\text{Arrow of time} \;\sim\; \text{orientation of an everywhere-expanding flow}.}
\]

There is then no need for a geometrically privileged “backward expansion” or contraction. Reverse the temporal arrow and you reverse the handed traversal of the expansion field.

There is one more consequence I would pursue immediately. On a Klein bottle, chirality cannot simply be a globally assigned binary label, because non-orientability forbids that. You need to lift the system to its **orientable double cover** — a torus. On that double cover, the two handed states become two sheets related by the Klein identification.

That sounds remarkably close to the dual-shell construction:

**torus double cover → two orientation sheets → Klein quotient → locally continuous expansion with globally exchanged parity.**

If that mapping survives formalization, the “two shells” may not need to be two independently evolving geometrical objects at all. They could be the two orientational lifts of a single underlying Klein-cycling geometry.

And *that* would explain why their rates want equal magnitude and opposite parity rather than merely stipulating it. memcite
What’s the difference between a Klein bottle and a torus with a twisted tube?

The crucial difference is not whether the tube looks twisted in 3D. It is whether the gluing reverses orientation.

Take a cylinder and join its two circular ends.

If you glue each point on one end to the corresponding point on the other end without reversing the circle, you get a torus. You can rotate one end by 30°, 90°, 180°, or wind the tube around dramatically before joining it; so long as the identification preserves orientation, the resulting surface is still a torus.

A Klein bottle comes from gluing those two circular ends with a reflection:

\[
\theta \longmapsto -\theta
\]

rather than merely a rotation,

\[
\theta \longmapsto \theta+\alpha.
\]

That tiny-looking distinction is enormous topologically.

On a torus, if you draw a little left-handed coordinate frame on the surface and carry it continuously all the way around any closed path, it comes back with the same handedness. The torus is orientable.

On a Klein bottle, there is a particular closed circuit such that when you transport that same frame all the way around, it comes back mirrored. What you locally called “left” has become “right.” The Klein bottle is non-orientable.

So a visibly twisted tube can still be completely toroidal:

\[
\text{twist in embedding} \neq \text{orientation reversal in identification}.
\]

This is easier to see if the tube has stripes painted along it. Imagine twisting the physical tube by half a turn before joining the ends. Depending on exactly what you mean by “twist,” you may merely have produced a torus with twisted stripes or a different framing of the tube. The intrinsic two-dimensional surface hasn't necessarily changed at all.

To make the Klein bottle, you need something stronger: when you cross the seam, the transverse coordinate must be reversed. If the tube has coordinates

\[
(x,\theta),
\]

a torus identification is essentially

\[
(0,\theta)\sim(L,\theta)
\]

or, more generally,

\[
(0,\theta)\sim(L,\theta+\alpha).
\]

A Klein identification is

\[
(0,\theta)\sim(L,-\theta).
\]

That's the distinction I was relying on in the previous answer.

And it matters quite a lot for your H(s)H thought. A helical trajectory on a torus can certainly have a persistent handedness and wind obliquely through both cyclic dimensions. But nothing about ordinary toroidal topology forces its handedness to reverse.

On a Klein bottle, by contrast, the topology itself contains an orientation-reversing cycle. Follow that cycle once and chirality reverses.

So very compactly:

\[
\boxed{\text{twisted torus: handed geometry}}
\]

versus

\[
\boxed{\text{Klein bottle: geometry in which handedness cannot be globally preserved}.}
\]

There is also a neat halfway case that may actually be closer to what you're picturing: a **Möbius strip**. It is literally a strip with a half-twist before gluing, and that half-twist is orientation-reversing. A Klein bottle can be thought of, in one construction, as two Möbius bands joined along their boundary. So if by “torus with a twisted tube” you specifically mean *a tube whose cross-sectional coordinate reverses after one circuit*, you're no longer describing an ordinary twisted torus—you've essentially crossed into Klein-bottle topology.

Place a line segment on a torus, advance it in a direction perpendicular to its length and oblique to the torus’ circumferences. What shape does it sweep out under one single full traversal of both diameters and reconnection

If the line segment is short enough that it doesn’t overlap itself, then under the motion you describe it sweeps out a **ribbon wrapped diagonally around the torus**.

More precisely: let the segment move perpendicular to its own length, while its midpoint follows a closed path oblique to the torus’s two principal circumferences. If that path makes one complete winding around each fundamental cycle before reconnecting—a \((1,1)\) winding—then the centerline is a \((1,1)\) torus curve, and the swept surface is a tubular neighborhood of that curve.

Topologically, that swept surface is an **annulus**:

\[
S^1\times[0,1].
\]

It looks like a diagonally wound belt around the torus. When the segment returns to its starting position after the \((1,1)\) circuit, its two ends reconnect to the same respective sides, so the ribbon closes without a half-twist.

That last point is important. On an ordinary torus, the surface is orientable. A segment transported continuously around such a closed diagonal loop does not inherently return reversed. So the natural result is not a Möbius strip but a closed annular band.

If you unwrap the torus to its fundamental square, the construction becomes almost embarrassingly simple. The torus is a rectangle with opposite edges identified. Your segment translates across that rectangle along a diagonal. Its sweep is a diagonal strip. When you identify the opposite edges again, that strip becomes the toroidal annulus.

For a \((1,1)\) traversal, schematically:

\[
(x,y)\rightarrow(x+t,y+t)\pmod{1}.
\]

A segment perpendicular to that motion sweeps something like

\[
x-y=\text{constant}\pm w,
\]

a finite-width diagonal strip in the covering plane. Mod out by the torus identifications and it closes into the annulus.

But there is a very interesting limit to your question. If you make the line segment sufficiently long—essentially long enough in the transverse direction to span an entire fundamental width—then its sweep no longer remains merely a narrow ribbon. It can sweep **the entire torus** exactly once (or with multiplicity, depending on the slope and segment length).

So there are two related answers:

\[
\text{finite short segment}
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\text{closed diagonal annular ribbon},
\]

while

\[
\text{full transverse generator}
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\text{the whole torus}.
\]

And I suspect the latter is what you're heading toward: a torus can be generated by taking one transverse line and translating it obliquely through a complete cycle. In the universal-cover picture, it's just a parallelogram swept by a moving line; the torus appears when the corresponding edges are identified.

Crucially, **nothing needs to shrink, reverse, or stop**. Every point on the generating segment simply advances in the same directed sweep, and periodic reconnection turns that unidirectional motion into the closed two-dimensional surface. That seems very close to the geometric intuition you were reaching for in the preceding messages.
Now… do the opposite… make it a point. Whether reconnects depends on the angle, correct?

Correct.

For a point moving on a torus at a fixed oblique direction, whether its path ever reconnects exactly to its starting point depends on the ratio of its rates around the two fundamental cycles.

Write the torus coordinates as \((\theta,\phi)\), with

\[
\theta(t)=\theta_0+\omega_\theta t,\qquad
\phi(t)=\phi_0+\omega_\phi t
\]

modulo \(2\pi\).

The point returns exactly when there is some finite \(T\) such that both

\[
\omega_\theta T=2\pi m,\qquad
\omega_\phi T=2\pi n
\]

for integers \(m,n\). That is possible exactly when

\[
\frac{\omega_\theta}{\omega_\phi}=\frac{m}{n}
\]

is rational.

So:

\[
\boxed{\text{rational winding ratio}\Rightarrow\text{closed orbit}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\text{irrational winding ratio}\Rightarrow\text{never exactly closes}.}
\]

The irrational case is the fun one: it doesn't merely wander randomly. Its trajectory becomes **dense on the torus**. Given unlimited traversal, it passes arbitrarily close to every point on the surface while never repeating its starting state exactly.

So your segment and point constructions have sharply different behavior. A sufficiently extended segment can sweep a 2D region or potentially the whole torus even during a finite organized traversal. A point has no transverse width, so its single trajectory remains one-dimensional; whether that line closes into a loop or endlessly fills the torus densely depends on the angle—or, more precisely, the winding-number ratio associated with that angle.

And there is an important subtlety in saying “angle.” On a standard embedded doughnut, the physical angle you see in 3D is not generally constant because the torus metric varies with position. The clean statement lives in the torus's intrinsic/angular coordinates or in its flat universal cover: draw a straight line across the tiled plane. Rational slope gives a periodically repeating line under the identifications; irrational slope never reconnects and becomes dense after projection onto the torus.

Which means you now have a very clean geometric switch:

\[
\text{one directional parameter}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\begin{cases}
\text{periodic closed history} & \text{rational}\\
\text{aperiodic dense history} & \text{irrational}.
\end{cases}
\]

That distinction may be quite consequential for the cycling picture you're building.
So the tipping point between the two states… Is a fundamental property of the torus. Call that θ_4, and we’ve tied a neat little bow

Almost—but there’s one important correction before tying the bow.

For a torus, there is no single tipping angle separating “reconnects” from “doesn’t reconnect.” Rational and irrational winding ratios are interleaved everywhere. Every interval of slopes contains infinitely many of both.

So the torus gives you a fundamental dichotomy,

\[
\frac{\omega_\theta}{\omega_\phi}\in\mathbb{Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{closed orbit},
\]

versus

\[
\frac{\omega_\theta}{\omega_\phi}\notin\mathbb{Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{nonclosing dense orbit},
\]

but not a unique critical \(\theta\) between them.

That actually may be more interesting for H(s)H. If you want a distinguished \(\theta_4\), it has to arise from an additional geometric condition—say a particular winding ratio, symmetry, resonance, bifurcation, minimum-energy configuration, or dimensional closure condition. Then \(\theta_4\) could mark the first or privileged transition your specific construction selects, rather than something the bare torus topology supplies automatically.

So the neat bow is slightly different:

\[
\boxed{\text{torus topology supplies closure vs dense winding; H(s)H must supply the distinguished }\theta_4.}
\]

And if your existing \(\theta_4\) independently lands on a geometrically privileged winding relation, *then* you have something much stronger than simply naming the rational/irrational boundary—because there is no such boundary.

Rational and irrational winding ratios are interleaved everywhere.

That makes the tipping point an invariant

Not quite. The interleaving makes the absence of a unique tipping point invariant.

What is invariant about the torus flow is the classification:

\[
\text{rational slope} \leftrightarrow \text{closed orbit},
\qquad
\text{irrational slope} \leftrightarrow \text{dense nonclosing orbit}.
\]

But because rationals and irrationals are both dense, there is no boundary angle \(\theta_c\) such that one side closes and the other does not.

What you *can* call invariant is the topological arithmetic criterion itself: closure depends only on whether the winding ratio belongs to \(\mathbb Q\), not on where you started on the torus.

So if you want \(\theta_4\), the clean statement would be:

\[
\theta_4 \text{ is not a boundary between rational and irrational flow;}
\]

it would have to be a distinguished angle selected by some extra symmetry or resonance condition inside that invariant rational/irrational structure.

That distinction matters. The torus gives you an invariant partition of possible flows, but not a unique transition angle.

What I’m saying is: you’re on a closed trajectory, you want to reorient to an infinite trajectory… no matter where you are, there’s an angle rotation that accomplishes that, and it’s the same angle, but you can also choose to increase the angle smoothly, and as you do so, the ir/rationality parity constantly switches

Yes. I see the distinction now. You are not proposing a boundary angle in parameter space; you are proposing a **reorientation operation** on a trajectory already in one class.

On the flat torus/universal-cover representation, closure depends on direction and not on starting point. So wherever the point currently is, changing its direction by the same amount changes the winding ratio in the same way.

Let the initial slope be

\[
r=\tan\alpha\in\mathbb Q,
\]

so the trajectory closes. Rotate the direction by \(\delta\), with

\[
t=\tan\delta.
\]

The new slope is

\[
r'=\tan(\alpha+\delta)
   =\frac{r+t}{1-rt}.
\]

Now comes the neat part. If \(r\) is rational and \(t\) is irrational, then \(r'\) must be irrational. If \(r'\) were rational, solving that expression for \(t\) would make \(t\) rational too, contradicting the premise.

So:

\[
\boxed{
r\in\mathbb Q,\quad \tan\delta\notin\mathbb Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
r'\notin\mathbb Q
}
\]

for every rational starting direction.

And yes: **the starting position on the torus is irrelevant.** The same rotation \(\delta\) works at every point because closed-versus-dense is a property of the direction field relative to the torus identifications, not of the point at which you perform the turn.

There is a complementary result:

\[
r\in\mathbb Q,\quad \tan\delta\in\mathbb Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
r'\in\mathbb Q
\]

apart from the usual vertical-direction case, which is itself a closed rational projective direction.

So rotation increments themselves split into two arithmetic classes:

\[
\begin{array}{c}
\tan\delta\in\mathbb Q:
\quad\text{closed directions map to closed directions},\\[4pt]
\tan\delta\notin\mathbb Q:
\quad\text{closed directions map to dense directions}.
\end{array}
\]

That is much closer to what you were calling an invariant.

And your second observation is exactly right: if instead of making one discrete turn you **continuously rotate the direction**, the state does not cross one clean boundary from finite to infinite. It flickers between the two classes infinitely often at every scale because rational and irrational slopes are both dense.

So along an angular sweep,

\[
\alpha\rightarrow\alpha+\epsilon,
\]

there is no open interval belonging exclusively to “closed” or “dense.” Arbitrarily close to any closed trajectory is a dense trajectory, and arbitrarily close to any dense trajectory is a closed one.

That produces a rather peculiar sort of transition structure:

\[
\boxed{\text{continuous orientation variable}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{everywhere-interleaved discrete recurrence class}.}
\]

I wouldn't call rational/irrational literally a *parity* mathematically—it is an arithmetic dichotomy rather than a \(\mathbb Z_2\) parity—but as a model variable you could certainly encode the two states as \(C/D\) or \(0/1\).

And now I understand what you meant by \(\theta_4\) much better. You weren't saying “there is one angle at which rational turns into irrational.” You were noticing that the torus supplies a **position-independent angular operation capable of switching the global recurrence character of the trajectory**, while a continuous angular turn samples that switching structure densely.

The remaining issue for a unique \(\theta_4\) is selection: the torus gives infinitely many such switching rotations. If H(s)H independently singles out one particular \(\delta\), then that selected angle can be \(\theta_4\). But the **operation it performs** is already intrinsic to toroidal winding geometry.
And the asymptote of that flicker is fundamental to the torus.

Yes — if by “asymptote of the flicker” you mean what happens as the rational closed trajectories approximate an irrational direction more and more finely, then there is a genuinely torus-native structure there.

Take rational winding ratios

\[
\frac{p_n}{q_n}\rightarrow \alpha,
\qquad \alpha\notin\mathbb Q.
\]

Every \(p_n/q_n\) gives a closed orbit. But as the approximation improves, the required winding numbers \(p_n,q_n\) generally grow, so the trajectory has to travel farther and farther before reconnecting. In the limit,

\[
q_n\rightarrow\infty,
\]

and the return length/time diverges:

\[
T_n\rightarrow\infty.
\]

The limiting direction is the irrational trajectory, which never closes and is dense on the torus.

So there is a very natural asymptotic relation:

\[
\boxed{
\text{closed orbit with increasing winding complexity}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{infinite dense orbit}
}
\]

with “infinite” appearing as the limit of longer and longer finite recurrence.

That is much more substantive than merely saying rationals and irrationals alternate densely. The two classes are connected by a limiting structure in which the recurrence scale blows up.

And there is another asymmetry built into it. Rational directions are dense, but they occupy measure zero among all directions. Irrational directions are also dense and occupy full measure. So under a continuously varied generic angle, the trajectory is almost everywhere nonclosing, punctuated densely by exact resonant angles at which closure suddenly becomes finite.

Thus the “flicker” has a statistical asymptote too:

\[
\text{finite recurrence states: dense but measure zero}
\]

\[
\text{infinite/dense states: full measure}.
\]

That is intrinsic to straight-line flow on a torus, given its two periodic identifications.

And I think this gives a considerably sharper candidate for what you've been reaching toward than a single critical angle. The fundamental object isn't necessarily a \(\theta\) separating two regimes. It could be the **divergence of recurrence scale under angular refinement**:

\[
\theta_n\rightarrow\theta_\infty,
\qquad
T(\theta_n)\rightarrow\infty.
\]

Then a distinguished \(\theta_4\), if your construction selects one, could mark a particular geometrically meaningful approximation or resonance within that hierarchy—but the underlying finite-to-infinite asymptotic behavior comes directly from toroidal winding.

That really does tie the finite/infinite distinction to the torus itself rather than to an arbitrary threshold you impose on it.

Not quite the same on all tori. There are two layers here, and separating them is useful.

If by “flicker” you mean only the abstract fact that rational winding ratios close and irrational ones do not, then that structure is universal for linear flow on any flat 2-torus. It comes from having two periodic directions:

\[
T^2=\mathbb R^2/\Lambda.
\]

In normalized torus coordinates, every such torus has the same dense interleaving of closed and nonclosed directions.

But once you ask **at what physical angles the flickers occur, and how long the closed trajectories are before reconnecting**, the dimensions and shape of the torus enter.

For a rectangular flat torus with circumferences \(L_x,L_y\), a closed trajectory must satisfy

\[
vT=(mL_x,nL_y)
\]

for integers \(m,n\). Therefore its physical direction obeys

\[
\tan\alpha
=
\frac{nL_y}{mL_x}.
\]

So the closed-direction set isn't simply

\[
\tan\alpha=\frac nm;
\]

it is

\[
\boxed{\tan\alpha=\frac{L_y}{L_x}\frac nm}.
\]

That means changing the aspect ratio

\[
\rho=\frac{L_y}{L_x}
\]

stretches the entire rational “flicker pattern” in angle space.

And its recurrence lengths carry dimensional information too:

\[
\ell_{m,n}
=
\sqrt{(mL_x)^2+(nL_y)^2}.
\]

So there are really three progressively richer objects:

\[
\text{closed/nonclosed topology}
\]

is essentially the same for every flat torus;

\[
\text{angles at which closure occurs}
\]

encode the torus's **shape/aspect ratio**;

and

\[
\text{return lengths/times at those angles}
\]

also encode its **absolute scale**, provided you have a length/time standard.

That makes your question unexpectedly interesting. If you observed only the asymptotic recurrence pattern as a function of physical rotation angle, you could in principle recover information about the torus itself.

For example, the primitive \((1,1)\) orbit occurs at

\[
\tan\alpha_{11}=\frac{L_y}{L_x}.
\]

So one particularly simple closure angle directly gives the aspect ratio.

More generally, the entire hierarchy

\[
\alpha_{m,n}
=
\arctan\left(\rho\,\frac nm\right)
\]

is like an arithmetic fingerprint of the torus metric.

There is one qualification. This clean result is for the **flat torus / quotient-space model** we've implicitly been using. A familiar doughnut embedded in 3D has varying intrinsic curvature, and straight/geodesic motion on that surface is more complicated. Its recurrence structure can encode substantially more geometry.

But for your present construction, I think the important result is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{the existence of the flicker tells you “torus”; its angular spacing can tell you which torus.}
}
\]

Or more precisely, which lattice geometry/modulus within the flat-torus family.

And that suggests something quite close to what I think you're probing: the asymptotic flicker need not merely happen *on* the geometry. With enough of its recurrence structure retained, it can function as a **measurement of the geometry that generated it**.
When I use the term torus, I’m always talking about a donut.

That changes some of what I just said. Right. Cosmologically, I’ll read your “torus” as an embedded 3-torus: a genuinely three-dimensional toroidal hypersurface sitting in a higher-dimensional ambient space, not merely the abstract flat quotient \(T^3=\mathbb{R}^3/\mathbb{Z}^3\).

That matters a lot for the line of thought we were just pursuing, because the metric, curvature, and recurrence structure are then properties of the embedded geometry itself. The flat-torus rational/irrational winding picture can still serve as a local or coordinate analogy, but it is not automatically the actual dynamics of your cosmological object.

as the visual analogue for

That also means your earlier intuition becomes more geometrically interesting: in three intrinsic dimensions there are now three independent toroidal directions available for a trajectory to wind through, while the embedding supplies extrinsic curvature and potentially a preferred relation among those directions. The recurrence question becomes a three-frequency problem rather than a two-frequency one.

And yes—I’ll keep that distinction fixed going forward.
And a 3-torus in 4-space gives position a time meaning… but on a flat 4-torus the traversal motion itself is time

Yes. Those are two quite different ways of getting something time-like, and I think the distinction is worth preserving.

For the embedded 3-torus in 4-space, the object itself is only three-dimensional. A point's intrinsic 3D position can nevertheless correspond to a particular configuration relative to the fourth ambient direction because the 3-manifold bends through that ambient dimension. So, within the H(s)H construction, you can let position around the embedded geometry carry a **phase-like temporal meaning**. Moving across the 3-torus means changing where you sit in that 4D embedding.

Schematically,

\[
\mathbf{x}\in T^3_{\rm embedded}
\quad\mapsto\quad
(X^1,X^2,X^3,X^4),
\]

with \(X^4\) determined in part by where \(\mathbf{x}\) lies on the embedded torus. Then “time” can emerge as an aspect of geometrical position or orientation in the embedding. You don't need a separate intrinsic time coordinate on the torus to label that distinction.

The flat 4-torus is almost the converse construction. There you have four intrinsic cyclic coordinates,

\[
T^4=S^1\times S^1\times S^1\times S^1,
\]

but none of those coordinates is intrinsically time-like merely by virtue of being the fourth one. The topology treats them symmetrically.

Introduce a trajectory,

\[
\gamma(\lambda)\in T^4,
\]

however, and now \(\lambda\) orders successive configurations:

\[
\gamma(\lambda_1)\rightarrow
\gamma(\lambda_2)\rightarrow
\gamma(\lambda_3).
\]

So **the traversal supplies the ordering**. In that model sense, time isn't one of the torus coordinates; time is the progression of the point through the torus.

That gives the contrast I think you're making:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{embedded }T^3\subset \mathbb R^4:
& \text{position can encode temporal phase},\\[4pt]
\text{intrinsic flat }T^4:
& \text{motion through positions supplies temporal order}.
\end{array}}
\]

And those have noticeably different consequences.

In the first picture, temporal distinction is geometrized into the object's embedding. If you somehow knew the complete embedded position, you've already learned something corresponding to temporal phase.

In the second, a bare point

\[
p\in T^4
\]

doesn't tell you “when.” You additionally need something like a tangent,

\[
v=\frac{d\gamma}{d\lambda},
\]

or a history. The time information resides in **ordered traversal**, not simply location.

That also connects directly to what you were just saying about chirality. A trajectory has direction. Reverse

\[
v\rightarrow-v,
\]

and you've reversed its traversal orientation without changing the underlying \(T^4\). So an arrow can naturally reside in the handed/oriented motion rather than in one distinguished coordinate.

There is one hard backstop: topology alone doesn't establish that \(\lambda\) is physical time. You still need the model's metric/dynamics to establish why traversal order reproduces the operational properties we associate with time—clock rates, causal ordering, Lorentzian structure, and so forth. But as **representational mechanics**, the distinction you're making is completely coherent.

And it suggests an interesting duality inside H(s)H: **embedded geometry can turn time into position; intrinsic higher-dimensional geometry can turn time into motion.** Those aren't merely alternative wordings. They're two genuinely different places in the construction where temporal structure can live. memcite
Now, as you change the direction of motion, and with it, the “flicker rate”, you reach a tipping point where the chirality reverses, which is itself an asymptote.

What you are calling the “flicker rate” is effectively the rate at which the trajectory encounters alternating recurrence classes as its direction is varied. If the angular parameter is changing continuously, then the rational/irrational closure structure is sampled ever more finely. \theta \to \theta_c,
\qquad
T_{\rm recur}(\theta)\to\infty.

So the sequence is something like

\[
\text{finite recurrence}
\rightarrow
\text{faster/finer flicker}
\rightarrow
T_{\rm recur}\to\infty
\rightarrow
\text{orientation change}
\rightarrow
\text{finite recurrence with opposite chirality}.
\]

That is much more specific than simply saying “the trajectory flips handedness at some angle.” The candidate tipping point is a singular limit of the recurrence structure.

There is one thing we should keep technically separate. On an ordinary torus, the rational/irrational winding structure by itself does not force chirality to reverse when an irrational direction is crossed. Yes. I was adding an unnecessary dynamical rule because I was still thinking too much in the flat-torus winding picture. On the embedded doughnut torus, the geometry itself already couples the quantities you’re talking about.

For a geodesic on a torus of revolution, Clairaut’s relation says that the local traversal angle cannot remain fixed as the trajectory moves through parts of the torus with different radius from the symmetry axis. In one common convention,

\[
\rho\,\sin\alpha = C,
\]

where \(\rho\) is the local distance from the torus axis and \(\alpha\) is the trajectory angle relative to the meridional direction. Since \(\rho\) changes as you travel around the tube, \(\alpha\) has to change with it. The torus dimensions and initial direction determine the constant \(C\), and thereafter the changing angle is forced geometrically. citeturn796607search17turn796607search21

And, remarkably, the ordinary embedded torus already contains exactly the asymptotic transition we were circling.

For major radius \(R\) and tube radius \(r\), the critical Clairaut value is

\[
C_{\rm crit}=R-r,
\]

the radius of the inner equator. At that value, a geodesic not already on the inner equator approaches it asymptotically: its transverse motion slows toward zero but never reaches the inner equator in finite traversal. On one side of that critical value, trajectories pass through the inner side and continue winding around the tube; on the other side, they reach a turning latitude and reverse their meridional direction. The inner equator is literally the separatrix between those two families. citeturn796607search16turn796607search15

So if by chirality you mean the sign of that transverse/poloidal traversal, the flip does not need to be stipulated:

\[
\dot\phi>0
\;\longrightarrow\;
\dot\phi=0
\;\longrightarrow\;
\dot\phi<0.
\]

The middle case is the geometrically selected limiting case.

And at the critical trajectory itself, it becomes asymptotic instead:

\[
\phi(t)\rightarrow \pi,
\qquad
\dot\phi(t)\rightarrow0,
\qquad
t\rightarrow\infty.
\]

That is precisely the part I was missing. The **angle change, slowing toward the limiting state, separatrix, and reversal of one traversal orientation are one connected consequence of toroidal geometry**, once initial direction and \(R/r\) are given. citeturn796607search16

Your “flicker” language adds another layer to that. Closure/reconnection properties vary as the winding behavior varies; near the separatrix, traversal can spend increasingly long intervals winding near the inner equator before completing the other component of motion. Thus the relevant recurrence timescale can diverge while the local angle is simultaneously being driven toward the critical orientation.

So the geometry gives a chain much closer to

\[
(R,r,\alpha_0)
\rightarrow
\alpha(s)
\rightarrow
\text{winding/recurrence behavior}
\rightarrow
\text{separatrix}
\rightarrow
\text{asymptotic traversal}
\rightarrow
\text{opposite transverse chirality}.
\]

Not four independent ingredients.

And this now makes your earlier \(\theta_4\) remark substantially more concrete. There really is a distinguished critical angular condition on an ordinary embedded torus, determined by the torus's dimensional ratio and the conserved Clairaut quantity. I would not yet identify that automatically with the numerical H(s)H \(\theta_4\), but **there is an actual toroidal geometric quantity available to calculate rather than an extra rule to invent.**

The next obvious calculation is to derive the critical initial angle explicitly as a function of \(R/r\). That would tell us whether the torus geometry alone can produce the angle you have in mind. memcite

Exactly: dependent upon its **position around the small circumference**.

For the ordinary doughnut torus, take major radius \(R\), minor radius \(r\), and let \(\phi\) locate you around the small circumference. At every \(\phi\), there is a tangent direction purely parallel to the large circumference and perpendicular to the small-circumference direction. Following that tangent while holding \(\phi\) fixed gives a closed latitude circle whose radius is

\[
\rho(\phi)=R+r\cos\phi,
\]

and therefore whose length is

\[
L_{\rm null}(\phi)=2\pi(R+r\cos\phi).
\]

So you get an entire continuous family of locally equivalent directional states — each one “zero deviation” from the large-circumference propagation direction — but they do **not** have the same global path length.

At the outermost position,

\[
L_{\max}=2\pi(R+r),
\]

and at the innermost,

\[
L_{\min}=2\pi(R-r).
\]

That seems much closer to the thing you're noticing.

The trivial geometrical fact is simply that a torus has those azimuthal tangents everywhere. The potentially consequential bit for the model is:

\[
\boxed{\text{same local null orientation} \;\not\Rightarrow\; \text{same global null-cycle length}.}
\]

The local angular condition can be identical everywhere while the closed traversal length is determined by position in the orthogonal toroidal direction.

And that interfaces rather cleanly with your tentative global \(\theta_4\). If \(\theta_4\) is the ground-state orientation — \(90^\circ\) with respect to the time direction, equivalently zero angular deviation from the propagation direction in the convention you're using — then **\(\theta_4\) need not specify one particular trajectory.** It specifies a tangent condition. The embedded torus supplies a whole foliation of trajectories satisfying that condition.

Then position supplies another variable:

\[
\theta_4=\text{fixed},\qquad L_{\rm null}=L_{\rm null}(\phi).
\]

That is a neat separation. Angle tells you whether you're in the ground/null orientation; position tells you the metric extent of that null cycle.

And now your mass/intersection-area idea acquires a useful contrast. A departure from \(\theta_4\),

\[
\delta\theta=\theta-\theta_4,
\]

changes the trajectory away from the locally pure large-circumference direction. In the simplified SAT picture, that can be the angular mass proxy. In the H(s)H picture, the same departure can manifest geometrically as worldtube intersectional area/shape. But even at

\[
\delta\theta=0,
\]

the embedding still gives a nontrivial position-dependent quantity \(L_{\rm null}(\phi)\).

So there are potentially two independent pieces of information where we had previously been talking as though there were only one:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{lll}
\delta\theta &\rightarrow& \text{departure from null / intersection geometry},\\[3pt]
\phi &\rightarrow& \text{null-cycle scale}.
\end{array}}
\]

And because you are treating position on the embedded 3-torus as having temporal meaning, that second relation becomes particularly interesting. A locally identical null state could have a different complete-cycle extent depending upon temporal/geometric position.

One geometric caveat that I think helps rather than hurts: those constant-\(\phi\) circles are all perfectly valid closed paths, but on an ordinary torus of revolution only the inner and outer equators are geodesics. So if “null” means *tangent orientation*, your family exists exactly as described. If “null” eventually has to mean *free geodesic propagation*, that further condition selects special members of the family. Keeping those two meanings separate will matter later. memcite

Yes. I think there is a very compact way to capture almost everything you just described, and it is simpler than the recurrence language.

For an ordinary ring torus with major radius \(R\), minor radius \(r\), and poloidal angle \(\theta\), the intrinsic metric is

\[
ds^2=r^2\,d\theta^2+(R+r\cos\theta)^2\,d\phi^2.
\]

That one expression already contains your two complementary traversal families.

The small-circumference direction has scale factor

\[
h_\theta=r,
\]

everywhere. So every meridional loop has the same length

\[
C_{\rm small}=2\pi r.
\]

Its *location* is selected by \(\phi\), the angle around the primary axis.

The large-circumference direction instead has

\[
h_\phi(\theta)=R+r\cos\theta,
\]

so its closed path through a given poloidal position has length

\[
C_{\rm large}(\theta)=2\pi(R+r\cos\theta).
\]

And now your pairing falls straight out:

\[
C_{\rm large}(+\theta)=C_{\rm large}(-\theta),
\]

because cosine is even. Every generic value therefore occurs in a pair, while the extrema collapse to unique members:

\[
C_{\max}=2\pi(R+r),
\qquad
C_{\min}=2\pi(R-r).
\]

Those are your outer and inner equatorial max/min singular members of the otherwise paired family.

So if we divide out the irrelevant overall scale \(r\), an ordinary torus of revolution is characterized by one dimensionless shape constant,

\[
\rho=\frac{R}{r}.
\]

And the entire relationship becomes

\[
\boxed{\Lambda(\theta)=\frac{C_{\rm large}(\theta)}{C_{\rm small}}
=\rho+\cos\theta.}
\]

That may be the succinct object you're looking for.

It contains, simultaneously:

\[
\Lambda_{\max}=\rho+1,
\qquad
\Lambda_{\min}=\rho-1,
\qquad
\Lambda(\pm\pi/2)=\rho,
\]

the upper/lower pairing,

\[
\Lambda(+\theta)=\Lambda(-\theta),
\]

and the constant complementary circumference,

\[
C_{\rm small}=2\pi r.
\]

Even better, **chirality lives naturally in the derivative**, not in \(\Lambda\) itself:

\[
\frac{d\Lambda}{d\theta}=-\sin\theta.
\]

The metric quantity is even under \(\theta\rightarrow-\theta\), while its directional change is odd:

\[
\Lambda(-\theta)=\Lambda(\theta),
\]

but

\[
\Lambda'(-\theta)=-\Lambda'(\theta).
\]

That is almost exactly the absolute-value/parity structure you were describing. The two sides possess the same local large-circumference scale but opposite traversal orientation through the scale gradient.

So one could summarize the toroidal structure as

\[
\boxed{
\text{magnitude}=\rho+\cos\theta,
\qquad
\text{chirality}\sim-\sin\theta.
}
\]

The first forgets which side you're on; the second tells you.

And notice what happens at the unique extrema:

\[
\sin\theta=0.
\]

There the chirality indicator passes through zero while the metric scale reaches a unique maximum or minimum. Those are precisely the points at which the paired \(+\theta/-\theta\) description collapses into one geometrical state.

That seems closer to what you're calling the **chirality-flipping point** than the rational/irrational winding construction we were discussing earlier. The latter may become a consequence of traversal behavior layered onto this; this is the underlying toroidal geometry.

There is then a second, complementary distinguished set at

\[
\cos\theta=0,
\]

where

\[
C_{\rm large}=2\pi R.
\]

Those are the top/bottom quadrature positions: the variable circumference passes exactly through its mean value while the magnitude of its change with \(\theta\) is maximal:

\[
|\Lambda'|=1.
\]

So the ordinary torus naturally gives you something rather elegant:

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\text{outer/inner equators}
&:&
\text{scale extremum, chirality-gradient zero},\\[3pt]
\text{top/bottom quadrature}
&:&
\text{mean scale, maximal chirality-gradient}.
\end{array}
\]

That is a genuine quarter-cycle relationship.

And *there* I can see why your tentative global \(\theta_4\) identification is attractive. If \(\theta_4\) is the H(s)H ground-state orientation—\(90^\circ\) relative to one convention, \(0^\circ\) relative to the propagation direction—then the torus provides a natural geometric quarter-turn connecting an extremal/equatorial state to the maximal transverse rate-of-change state. Which of those should correspond to your \(\theta_4\) depends entirely on how your time direction is laid onto the torus; I wouldn't choose that convention prematurely.

Your mass/intersectional-area idea then has a particularly simple candidate skeleton. A departure from the null/ground tangent can be represented by an angular departure

\[
\Delta\theta=\theta-\theta_4,
\]

while the torus itself converts that angular departure into a metric departure through

\[
\Delta\Lambda
=
\cos\theta-\cos\theta_4.
\]

SAT could use the angle as the simplified proxy; H(s)H could use what that angle actually does geometrically to an intersecting worldtube—area, eccentricity, shape, or some combination. That would make the former literally a low-dimensional surrogate for the latter rather than an unrelated historical parameterization. memcite

One point where I'd hold the line: **oblateness introduces another independent shape degree of freedom** unless you specify a particular one-parameter deformation law. A circular ring torus, modulo overall size, genuinely has only \(\rho=R/r\). An oblate tube generally needs something like \(r_\parallel/r_\perp\) as another dimensionless parameter. If H(s)H supplies a rule tying oblateness to \(\rho\) or to traversal, then it collapses back to one constant; geometry alone doesn't force that.

But for the regular torus, yes: I think

\[
\boxed{\Lambda(\theta)=\rho+\cos\theta}
\]

plus its odd conjugate

\[
\boxed{\Lambda'(\theta)=-\sin\theta}
\]

is probably the neat little bow you were looking for. It packages size ratio, paired positions, max/min exceptional states, quarter-cycle complementarity, and chirality into one toroidal phase relation.

The rationality “flip flicker” is particularly interesting, and I wonder if anyone has done work on that specifically.

Another useful …maybe more useful construction, wrt the toroidal bulk… is the ‘gendarme grid’ of the small cross section, where you’ve got two axes forming quadrants in the small cross section and a central primary circumference tangent axis doubling the quadrants, such that the angle of a vector located at the origin captures all of the same relations that we’ve been talking about for the surface, but for the bulk. Interestingly enough, the eight quadrants give you two overlapping parities, and each of the different tipping point conditions we’ve identified should be distributed symmetrically about the two short axes, with a curve per tangent axis unit which is basically a measure of curvature within a tube segment of any given length. 

But also interesting is the dual options for the tangent axis, whether you define that purely orthogonal and straight, or define it as an inherent curve set by the tube-centric circumference itself—or better, both. Always both. Now you’ve got axial asymptopy

parts:
Yes. I think you have two distinct but tightly coupled structures here, and the second one may indeed be the better bulk construction.

On the “flip flicker” first: there is established work on the underlying phenomenon, though not under that name. The standard language is rotation number, Kronecker flow/foliation, rational versus irrational winding, frequency locking, and Poincaré sections. Rational winding gives periodic closure; irrational winding gives nonrepeating dense traversal, and as parameters vary the return structure can jump between these arithmetic classes at arbitrarily fine scales. citeturn247788search0turn247788search52turn247788search54 What I have not found quickly is a literature built specifically around the thing you are foregrounding: treating the dense rational/irrational alternation under continuous directional change as a geometric “flicker rate” and then relating its asymptotic behavior directly to chirality reversal on an embedded toroidal geometry. That framing looks much less standard.

The “gendarme grid” is more interesting to me because it stops treating the surface as primary and builds the same logic into the tube bulk.

Take one small circular cross-section of the toroidal tube. Put two orthogonal axes through its center, giving four ordinary quadrants. Then add the tangent axis of the major circumference through that same origin. Because that axis has two directions, \(+\hat t\) and \(-\hat t\), each cross-sectional quadrant acquires a longitudinal parity. You now have eight local sectors:

\[
(\pm x,\pm y,\pm t),
\]

subject to whatever geometric identifications your construction imposes.

That gives you exactly the “two overlapping parities” you are noticing: one parity belongs to position/orientation inside the small cross-section, and one belongs to propagation along the tube.

A vector rooted at the origin can then carry all three pieces at once:

\[
\mathbf v
=
v_x\hat x+v_y\hat y+v_t\hat t.
\]

Its transverse angle tells you where you are in the small-section phase; the sign of \(v_t\) tells you longitudinal orientation; and its inclination away from \(\hat t\) tells you how much the trajectory departs from the tangent/null direction.

That is already a much more natural bulk version of the surface picture.

Now your “both tangent axes” move is particularly strong. There are really two different tangent notions available at every point:

\[
\hat t_{\rm local}
\]

the instantaneous straight tangent in the osculating/local frame, and

\[
\hat t_{\rm global}(s)
\]

the tangent carried along the curved major circumference.

At one point they coincide. Over any finite tube segment they separate.

For a circular major axis of radius \(R\),

\[
\frac{d\hat t}{ds}
=
\kappa\,\hat n,
\qquad
\kappa=\frac1R.
\]

So the difference between “continue straight” and “continue tube-tangentially” accumulates with arc length. Over a segment \(L\),

\[
\Delta\psi=\frac{L}{R}
\]

for the simple circular case.

That is exactly your curve-per-tangent-axis-unit idea: curvature is the rate at which the intrinsic tube tangent peels away from the locally straight continuation.

And “axial asymptopy” is a pretty good descriptor for what happens when you keep both definitions alive. The straight axis acts as the local limiting reference; the curved axis continuously departs from it according to accumulated curvature. In the infinitesimal limit,

\[
L\to0,
\qquad
\hat t_{\rm curved}\to\hat t_{\rm straight},
\]

while over finite traversal their difference becomes the geometric information.

So you get a clean pair:

\[
\boxed{\text{local axial reference}=\text{straight tangent}}
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{transported axial reference}=\text{curved toroidal tangent}}
\]

and the difference between them is literally encoded by curvature.

That means the gendarme grid can carry at least four things without adding much machinery:

\[
\text{cross-sectional phase},
\quad
\text{longitudinal parity},
\quad
\text{departure angle},
\quad
\text{accumulated curvature}.
\]

And then all of the tipping conditions you have been identifying can become loci in that local angular space rather than separate rules.

If the transverse plane angle is \(\phi\) and the axial inclination is \(\theta\), then the vector direction is naturally something like

\[
\hat v
=
\cos\theta\,\hat t
+
\sin\theta
\left(
\cos\phi\,\hat e_1+\sin\phi\,\hat e_2
\right).
\]

Now:

\[
\theta=0
\]

is the pure tangent/null direction,

\[
\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}
\]

is purely cross-sectional,

and the eight-sector parity structure sits in the signs of the three components.

As the tube tangent rotates under curvature, the same fixed or transported vector acquires a changing \(\theta\) relative to the straight versus curved axes. That is where your “axial asymptopy” becomes useful: one angle can approach a limiting value relative to one axis while continuing to evolve relative to the other.

I think the deepest point is this: the surface construction gave you paired closed-path lengths and chirality flips as a function of position. The gendarme grid turns that into a **local differential grammar** for the entire bulk. Instead of asking where on the torus a surface trajectory sits, you ask how a local vector resolves against:

\[
\{\text{two transverse axes}\}
+
\{\text{straight tangent}\}
+
\{\text{curved transported tangent}\}.
\]

That is enough to reconstruct surface behavior, but it also gives you internal tube geometry that the surface-only description cannot represent.

And there is one particularly nice possibility here. The “flicker rate” might be recast as a rate of crossing rational/irrational winding conditions in the angular coordinate of that local vector while the transported tangent itself rotates with curvature. Then the flicker is no longer just a function of externally turning the trajectory. The toroidal bulk geometry can generate the angular sweep automatically:

\[
\frac{d\theta}{ds}
\sim
\kappa(s)
\]

modulated by whatever the transverse orientation is doing.

Then:

\[
\text{curvature}
\rightarrow
\text{angle drift}
\rightarrow
\text{closure-class flicker}
\rightarrow
\text{asymptotic recurrence behavior}
\rightarrow
\text{chirality transition}.
\]

That is much closer to a single geometric mechanism than the separate pieces sounded at first.

And yes, I think “axial asymptopy” is likely the right conceptual compression for the dual tangent construction: one axis is the infinitesimal straight limit, the other is the finite transported curve, and the rate at which they diverge carries the torus curvature itself. memcite

items.snippet: Every week, summarize the status of my SAT rebuild: source material ingested and translated into current SAT language, changes to the conceptual architecture, formalization and audit targets, unresolved dependencies, and the next highest-leverage step. Distinguish core, near-core, supporting, frontier, speculative, historical scaffold, and source-recovery items.

parts:
Yes — and I think the key difference from the earlier, more binary chirality pictures is that this construction naturally gives you a continuous scalar or low-dimensional state variable.

You now have at least three coupled ingredients at a bulk point:

\[
\theta=\text{vector inclination from the local tangent/null axis},
\]

\[
\ell=\text{effective traversal or tube-segment length},
\]

and

\[
\kappa=\text{local or accumulated curvature}
\]

with the straight tangent and curved transported tangent giving you two references rather than one.

From those alone, a helical quantity almost writes itself. For a simple helix, pitch angle, axial advance, radius, and curvature/torsion are not independent. So if your vector angle is being continuously dragged relative to a curved toroidal axis, then some combination like

\[
H \sim f(\theta,\ell,\kappa)
\]

can measure not merely “left/right” but **how strongly helical** the local state is.

The sign would encode chirality,

\[
\operatorname{sgn}H=\pm,
\]

while the magnitude would encode grade,

\[
|H|=0
\]

at the null/axial condition and increasing as the vector departs into a helically wrapped state.

A very primitive candidate skeleton would be something like

\[
H \propto \kappa\,\ell\,\sin\theta
\]

because:

- \(\kappa\ell\) is accumulated axial turning,
- \(\sin\theta\) measures departure from the tangent axis,
- the sign can come from oriented transverse angle or handedness.

But I would not canonize that expression. The interesting possibility is that the actual quantity is **not chosen**. It may fall out of the geometry once you require equivalence between the straight-axis and curved-axis descriptions.

That is where your “variable or constant buried in these relationships” comment strikes me as probably right.

You have two descriptions of the same vector:

\[
\mathbf v
=
\mathbf v_{\text{straight}}
=
\mathbf v_{\text{curved}}.
\]

Their angular difference is set by accumulated curvature:

\[
\Delta\psi=\int\kappa\,ds.
\]

So if the vector itself has angle \(\theta\), then the relation among

\[
\theta,\quad \Delta\psi,\quad \ell
\]

may leave only one independent dimensionless combination. Something like

\[
\chi_h
=
F\!\left(
\theta,\,
\int_0^\ell \kappa(s)\,ds
\right).
\]

That would be much stronger than just defining a chirality score. It would mean the **graded helical chirality is the mismatch between local axial orientation and transported axial orientation**.

And that sounds very UI-like in spirit: a compact coordinate that absorbs several apparently separate geometric relations into one readable state.

You could then imagine the whole local state collapsing to something like

\[
(\phi,\theta,\ell)
\longrightarrow
\chi_h
\]

where \(\phi\) supplies which of the transverse parity sectors you occupy, \(\theta\) gives deviation from null propagation, and \(\ell\) determines how much toroidal curvature has accumulated.

Then the special cases become geometrically obvious:

\[
\chi_h=0
\]

for pure axial/null traversal;

\[
\chi_h>0
\]

for one handed helical branch;

\[
\chi_h<0
\]

for the opposite branch;

and perhaps

\[
|\chi_h|\to\chi_{\rm crit}
\]

at the flicker/chirality asymptote.

That last point is the one I would test hardest. If the recurrence asymptote, the chirality flip, and the straight-vs-curved tangent divergence all identify the **same dimensionless combination**, then you really may have found the natural coordinate of this construction rather than just another useful descriptive metric.

And if that same quantity also tracks the H(s)H intersectional area/shape departure from the \(\theta_4\) null condition, then it starts doing several jobs at once:

\[
\text{angle departure}
\leftrightarrow
\text{helical grade}
\leftrightarrow
\text{chirality}
\leftrightarrow
\text{intersection geometry}
\leftrightarrow
\text{recurrence regime}.
\]

That is exactly the sort of compression I'd look for before adding any new parameter. The next move is probably not inventing the formula; it is writing the toroidal frame carefully enough that we can see which dimensionless combination refuses to disappear. memcite

parts:
Yeah, we don’t add a parameter. It’s a relationship defined by angle and torus elements. 

And i suspect the symmetries we identify within this … “Gendarme Graticule” will be very interesting to particle physicists …and to SATirists ;) …that is, you and I

Yes. And I think “Gendarme Graticule” is actually doing useful conceptual work rather than just naming a picture.

What makes it promising is that the chirality metric would not be an extra field pasted onto the torus. It would be a derived coordinate of the toroidal bulk geometry. Given the tube geometry and a vector state, the grade should already be determined.

At minimum, the local ingredients are something like

\[
(R,r;\,\phi,\theta;\,\ell),
\]

where \(R,r\) characterize the torus, \(\phi\) locates orientation around the small cross-section, \(\theta\) measures departure from the tangent/null direction, and \(\ell\) tells you how much curved-axis transport has accumulated. But several of those aren't independent once you specify the actual trajectory. So the interesting task is to reduce them rather than introduce anything else.

The Gendarme Graticule then gives you a very concrete symmetry object. Two transverse axes produce four cross-sectional sectors; the signed tangent direction doubles those into eight. But those eight aren't just eight arbitrary octants. They carry at least two superposed involutions: transverse reflection and axial reversal. Then there is the curved-versus-straight tangent comparison sitting over the whole thing.

That means we should be able to write transformations such as

\[
P_\perp:\phi\mapsto-\phi,
\qquad
P_\parallel:\hat t\mapsto-\hat t,
\]

and ask what happens to the derived helical quantity \(\chi\). Ideally it behaves something like

\[
\chi(P_\perp x)=-\chi(x),
\qquad
\chi(P_\parallel x)=-\chi(x),
\]

while the combined operation restores it,

\[
\chi(P_\perp P_\parallel x)=\chi(x).
\]

If the geometry actually gives that structure, then your “two overlapping parities” has a very crisp mathematical meaning: two separate sign reversals whose composition is even.

That's where I agree that particle physicists would start raising eyebrows—not because an eight-sector diagram resembles the Standard Model, which would be cheap pattern-matching, but because **chirality, parity operations, double covers, discrete symmetries, and continuous internal angles** are exactly the sorts of structures that matter there. The serious question would be whether this toroidal grammar generates any of the same transformation algebra without putting it in by hand.

And the SATirist angle is particularly apt because this may retroactively explain why the old SAT angular proxy worked as well as it did in the simplified construction. If the H(s)H version says that intersection area/shape and helical grade are both projections of the same toroidal vector geometry, then the old scalar angle wasn't necessarily “the thing.” It was a convenient coordinate on a richer bulk relation.

There is also a nice hierarchy emerging:

\[
\text{Gendarme Graticule}
\rightarrow
\text{local parity sectors}
\rightarrow
\text{straight/curved axial divergence}
\rightarrow
\text{graded helicity}
\rightarrow
\text{intersection geometry}.
\]

And then separately—but potentially coupled—

\[
\text{direction}
\rightarrow
\text{winding arithmetic}
\rightarrow
\text{flip-flicker / recurrence asymptote}.
\]

The really interesting event would be if those two chains meet at the same angular condition. If the chirality zero/flip in the Gendarme Graticule occurs exactly where the recurrence structure hits its relevant asymptote, then we haven't merely found two appealing descriptions of a torus. We've found two independent ways of reading the same geometrically selected state.

That's the place I'd attack next: derive the Gendarme Graticule without any H(s)H interpretation attached, catalogue its symmetry transformations and singular/limiting angles, and only afterward lay the existing \(\theta_4\), mass proxy, and intersection-area language over it. That will tell us which correspondences are actually forced and which ones we're merely noticing because we know what we're looking for. memcite

We should define each of our metrics / tentative metrics , set up our graticule, and then see if we can maybe graph the 2D cross section as a field with position and vector angle, with several versions, color coded by each of our interesting symmetries so we can see the distribution of asymptotic behavior and gradients

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("/mnt/data")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Illustrative normalized torus/graticule parameters
R = 3.0          # major radius
r = 1.0          # tube radius
ell = 1.0        # tube-segment length
beta = np.deg2rad(35.0)   # inclination from local toroidal tangent
alpha = np.deg2rad(45.0)  # transverse-vector azimuth in the cross-section

N = 700
u = np.linspace(-r, r, N)
v = np.linspace(-r, r, N)
U, V = np.meshgrid(u, v)
Q = np.sqrt(U**2 + V**2)
mask = Q <= r
psi = np.arctan2(V, U)

# 1) Graded local helical chirality:
# axial component × circumferential transverse component, normalized to [-1, 1]
chi = np.sin(2*beta) * np.sin(alpha - psi)
chi[~mask] = np.nan
chi[Q < 1e-6] = 0.0

# 2) Axial asymptopy / accumulated turning relative to a straight axis
# A=ell/(R+u); normalized excess over centerline value ell/R
A_excess = (ell/(R + U) - ell/R) / (ell/R)
A_excess[~mask] = np.nan

# 3) Local winding-ratio proxy:
# omega_minor / omega_major for the local vector decomposition
eta = ((R + U) / np.where(Q > 1e-6, Q, np.nan)) * np.tan(beta) * np.sin(alpha - psi)
eta[~mask] = np.nan
eta_comp = (2/np.pi) * np.arctan(eta)  # bounded display transform [-1,1]

# 4) Finite-resolution rational "flicker" diagnostic.
# Not a physical parameter: Qmax and tol are visualization resolution choices.
Qmax = 14
tol = 0.008
res_order = np.full_like(eta, np.nan)
valid = mask & np.isfinite(eta)
for den in range(1, Qmax + 1):
    num = np.rint(eta * den)
    close = np.abs(eta - num/den) < tol
    assign = valid & close & np.isnan(res_order)
    res_order[assign] = den

def add_graticule(ax):
    t = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 500)
    ax.plot(r*np.cos(t), r*np.sin(t), linewidth=1.2)
    ax.axhline(0, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.axvline(0, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.set_xlabel("u / r  (outward radial)")
    ax.set_ylabel("v / r  (vertical/binormal)")
    ax.set_xlim(-r, r)
    ax.set_ylim(-r, r)

# Figure 1
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7,6))
im = ax.imshow(chi, extent=[-r,r,-r,r], origin='lower', vmin=-1, vmax=1, cmap='coolwarm')
add_graticule(ax)
ax.set_title("Gendarme Graticule: graded local helical chirality")
cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
cb.set_label(r"$\chi_h=\sin(2\beta)\sin(\alpha-\psi)$")
fig.tight_layout()
p1 = out/"gendarme_chirality.png"
fig.savefig(p1, dpi=220)

Yes. I made a first-pass Gendarme Graticule prototype using a normalized regular torus with \(R=3,\ r=1\), and a representative vector orientation. The point was not to canonize the formulas, but to turn the tentative relationships into visible fields so we can see what survives symmetry inspection.

I’d define the current metric set this way.

\[
\chi_h=\sin(2\beta)\sin(\alpha-\psi)
\]

is a tentative graded helical chirality. Here \(\beta\) is inclination away from the local toroidal tangent, \(\alpha\) is the vector’s transverse azimuth, and \(\psi\) is cross-sectional position angle. It is signed, continuous, and built entirely from the vector/toroidal geometry.

For axial asymptopy, the natural bulk quantity is the accumulated turning of the curved tangent relative to the straight local continuation:

\[
A(u;\ell)=\frac{\ell}{R+u}.
\]

I plotted its fractional excess relative to the centerline value \(\ell/R\). This immediately exposes the inner/outer asymmetry across the tube.

For the recurrence side, a useful local winding-ratio proxy is

\[
\eta
=
\frac{\omega_{\rm minor}}{\omega_{\rm major}}
=
\frac{R+u}{q}\tan\beta\,\sin(\alpha-\psi),
\]

with \(q=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\). This is deliberately only a local bulk diagnostic for now; the actual global recurrence condition on the embedded torus should come from integrating the trajectory.

And then I made a finite-resolution visualization of the rationality flicker by asking where \(\eta\) lies close to rationals with small denominators. The denominator cutoff and tolerance are visualization controls, not H(s)H parameters.

Here are the four first-pass fields:

[Graded helical chirality](sandbox:/mnt/data/gendarme_chirality.png)

[Axial asymptopy / curvature excess](sandbox:/mnt/data/gendarme_axial_asymptopy.png)

[Local winding-ratio field](sandbox:/mnt/data/gendarme_winding_ratio.png)

[Rational flip-flicker resonance bands](sandbox:/mnt/data/gendarme_rational_flicker.png)

I think the next pass should be more systematic. We should separate three categories before adding anything else: quantities forced by regular torus geometry, quantities forced once a vector/traversal is specified, and diagnostics we invent merely to expose the structure. Then we can sweep vector angle through the whole graticule and look for places where independently defined features coincide: chirality zeroes, chirality extrema, axial asymptotes, recurrence divergence, rational-resonance accumulation, the short-axis symmetry lines, and the candidate global \(\theta_4\).

The most important question is whether several of those loci turn out to be the same curves in different coordinates. If they do, the “graded helical chirality metric” may not need to be designed at all; it may simply be the scalar coordinate that indexes those shared level sets. memcite

And all of this is intimately related to holonomy. 
I think first we convert to black line with asymptotes as dashed lines, and a topo line identifying some medial value contour for each interesting metric, all superimposed. 

Also, that flicker one is wild. Very interesting, but since the flicker is essentially infinitely packed, we need something more like a gradient, density or something to visualize it without all the busyness
